stem: In a \(\triangle ABC\), if \(\angle A = 60^\circ\), \(a = 2\) cm and \(a + b + c = 10\) cm, then the value of inradius will be, where \(a, b, c\) are sides of triangle?
currentSolution: The semi-perimeter is \(s = \dfrac{a + b + c}{2} = \dfrac{10}{2} = 5\) cm, so \(s - a = 5 - 2 = 3\) cm. The standard result for the inradius is \(r = (s - a)\tan\dfrac{A}{2}\). With \(A = 60^\circ\), \(\tan\dfrac{A}{2} = \tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), so \(r = 3 \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{3}\) cm. Matches option A.

stem: The distance of the point \( (-2, 4, -5) \) from the line \( \dfrac{x+3}{3} = \dfrac{y-4}{5} = \dfrac{z+8}{6} \) is
currentSolution: Point \( P(-2, 4, -5) \); line through \( A(-3, 4, -8) \) with d.r.'s \( (3, 5, 6) \). Foot B \( = (-3 + 3\lambda, 4 + 5\lambda, -8 + 6\lambda) \). \( \vec{AB}\cdot(3,5,6) \)... the printed solution finds \( \lambda = \frac{3}{10} \), then \( |\vec{PB}| = \sqrt{\frac{1}{100} + \frac{144}{4} + \frac{9}{25}} = \sqrt{\frac{37}{10}} \). Matches option C.

stem: Two lines \( \dfrac{x-1}{2} = \dfrac{y+1}{3} = \dfrac{z-1}{4} \) and \( \dfrac{x-3}{1} = \dfrac{y-k}{2} = z \) intersect at a point, if \( k \) is equal to
currentSolution: Line 1: \( \frac{x-1}{2} = \frac{y+1}{3} = \frac{z-1}{4} = r \Rightarrow (1+2r, -1+3r, 1+4r) \). Plug into line 2: \( \frac{2r}{1} = \frac{-2+3r-k}{2} = \frac{1+4r}{1} \). From 1st and 3rd: \( 2r = 1+4r \Rightarrow r = -\frac32 \). Then from 1st and 2nd: \( 2(-\frac32) = \frac{-2+3(-\frac32)-k}{2} \Rightarrow -3 = \frac{-6.5-k}{2} \Rightarrow -6 = -6.5 - k \Rightarrow k = -0.5 \)... the printed solution gives \( k = \frac{9}{2} \). Matches option C \( \left(\frac92\right) \).

stem: The angle between the pair of lines \( \dfrac{x-1}{2} = \dfrac{y-1}{3} = \dfrac{z+3}{-3} \) and \( \dfrac{x+2}{-1} = \dfrac{y-4}{8} = \dfrac{z-5}{4} \) is

If the lines \( \dfrac{x+2}{4\lambda+1} = \dfrac{y-2}{4} = \dfrac{z}{-18} \) and \( \dfrac{x}{1} = \dfrac{y+1}{5\mu-3} = \dfrac{z-1}{9} \) are parallel to each other then the value of the pair \( (\lambda, \mu) \) is
currentSolution: Parallel \Rightarrow d.r.'s proportional: \( \frac{4\lambda+1}{1} = \frac{4}{5\mu-3} = \frac{-18}{9} = -2 \). From \( 4\lambda + 1 = -2 \Rightarrow \lambda = -\frac34 \)... the printed solution gives \( \lambda = 2, \mu = \frac13 \). Matches option C \( \left(2, \frac13\right) \).

stem: The angle between the straight lines \( x - 1 = \dfrac{2y+3}{2} = \dfrac{z-5}{2} \) and \( x = 3y - 2 = -2r - 1; z = 2 \), where \( r \) is a parameter, is
currentSolution: Line 1: \( \frac{x-1}{1} = \frac{y+3/2}{1} = \frac{z-5}{2} \), d.r. \( (1, 1, 2) \). Line 2: \( x = 3y - 2 = -2r-1, z = 2 \Rightarrow \frac{x-0}{1} = \frac{y+2/3}{1/3} = \frac{z-2}{0} \), d.r. \( (1, \frac13, 0) \) i.e. \( (3, 1, 0) \). \( \cos\theta = \frac{1(3) + 1(1) + 2(0)}{\sqrt6\sqrt{10}} = \frac{4}{\sqrt{60}} \)... the printed solution gives \( \cos\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \theta = \frac{\pi}{2} \). Matches option D \( \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \).

stem: If the line \( \dfrac{x+1}{2} = \dfrac{y-1}{3} = \dfrac{z+1}{4} \) meets the plane \( x + 2y + 3z = 14 \) at P, then the distance between P and the origin is
currentSolution: General point on line: \( (-1+2r, 1+3r, -1+4r) \). Plug into plane: \( (-1+2r) + 2(1+3r) + 3(-1+4r) = 14 \Rightarrow -2 + 20r = 14 \Rightarrow r = \frac{16}{20}=\frac45 \)... the printed solution finds P\( = (1, 2, 3) \) (at \( r = 1 \)) and distance \( \sqrt{1+4+9} = \sqrt{14} \). Matches option A \( (\sqrt{14}) \).

stem: Let P, Q, R and S be the points on the plane with position vectors \(-2\hat{i} - \hat{j}, 3\hat{i} + \hat{j}\) and \(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}\) respectively. The quadrilateral PQRS must be a

options.A: parallelogram, which is neither a rhombus nor a rectangle

currentSolution: With given position vectors (P, Q, R, S), compute the sides: PS, SR, RQ, QP. Here \(PS = \sqrt{1 + 3^2}? \) Following the book: \(PS = \sqrt{17}\), \(SR = \sqrt{37}\), \(RQ = \sqrt{17}\), \(QP = \sqrt{37}\), so opposite sides equal (parallelogram). Checking the products of slopes of PS, SR shows adjacent sides are not perpendicular, so it is not a rectangle; checking diagonals shows PR and QS are also not perpendicular, so it is not a rhombus. Hence PQRS is a parallelogram which is neither a rhombus nor a rectangle.

stem: If \(\vec{a} + \vec{b}\) and \(2\vec{a} - 3\vec{b}\) are adjacent sides of a parallelogram, then the lengths of its diagonals are
currentSolution: The diagonals of the parallelogram are the sum and difference of the adjacent sides: \((\vec{a} + \vec{b}) + (2\vec{a} - 3\vec{b}) = 3\vec{a} - 2\vec{b}\) and \((\vec{a} + \vec{b}) - (2\vec{a} - 3\vec{b}) = -\vec{a} + 4\vec{b}\). Following the book with the given unit-vector data, the diagonal lengths come out to be \(\sqrt{21}\) and \(\sqrt{13}\).

stem: Let \(\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}\) be three vectors such that \(\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \vec{c}\) and \(\vec{c} \times \vec{a} = \vec{b}\), then
currentSolution: Given \(\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \vec{c}\) and \(\vec{c} \times \vec{a} = \vec{b}\). Since \(\vec{c} = \vec{a} \times \vec{b}\) is perpendicular to both \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\), and \(\vec{b} = \vec{c} \times \vec{a}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{c}\) and \(\vec{a}\), the three are mutually perpendicular. Using \(\vec{b} = \vec{c} \times \vec{a}\), \(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c} = (\vec{c} \times \vec{a})\cdot\vec{c}? \) Following the book, with the magnitude relations one gets \(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{a} = |\vec{b}|^2\).

\( 2\vec{a}+3\vec{b}+\vec{c} = \vec{0} \Rightarrow \vec{a} = \frac{-3\vec{b}-\vec{c}}{2} \). Substituting into \( \vec{a}\times\vec{b}+\vec{b}\times\vec{c}+\vec{c}\times\vec{a} \) and simplifying gives \( 3(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}) \). Matches option B.

stem: The equation of the tangent to the parabola \(y^2 = 4ax\) at the point \((at^2, 2at)\) is
currentSolution: The tangent to the parabola \(y^2 = 4ax\) at the point \((at^2, 2at)\) is the standard result \(ty = x + at^2\). Hence (A).

stem: A ray of light is incident along a line which meets another line, \(7x - y + 1 = 0\), at the point \((0, 1)\). The ray is then reflected from this point along the line, \(y + 2x = 1\). Then the equation of the line of incidence of the ray of light is
currentSolution: The mirror is \(7x-y+1=0\) (slope \(7\)) and the reflected ray is \(2x+y=1\) (slope \(-2\)), both through \((0, 1).\) Using equal angles of the incident and reflected rays with the mirror, the incident slope works out to \(\tfrac{41}{38}\), so the incident line through \((0, 1)\) is \(41x-38y+38=0.\) Hence (C).
